intro: A voicemail said your account will be auto-charged $499.99 today unless you call this number to cancel. You are calling it back now.

n1.speaker: caller
lines: Thank you for calling SecureGuard Billing, this is Daniel.
I can see an automatic renewal of $499.99 scheduled on your account for today. Were you calling to cancel that?

choices.label: Yes, I never authorised any renewal — cancel it
How did you even get my details? I never signed up
Hang up and check my real card statement myself

n2.speaker: caller
lines: Not a problem at all, I can process a full refund right now.
To do that I just need to connect to your computer. Please go to the website I'll read out and install our quick support tool so I can push the refund through.

choices.label: Okay, I'll install the support tool
Can't you just refund the card directly?
I'm not installing anything. I'll call my bank on the number on my card

n2b.speaker: caller
lines: It's linked to the email on your renewal notice, sir. Let's just get this refunded for you.
First I need to verify your identity — can you read me the one-time code we just texted to your phone?

choices.label: I will never read out a one-time code

n3.speaker: caller
lines: Unfortunately our system can't push a refund to the card directly, that's exactly why I need remote access.
It only takes a minute. Shall I send you the download link now?

choices.label: No. A real company doesn't need to control my computer to refund me

e-safe-hangup.title: You hung up and checked for yourself
e-safe-hangup.explanation: You didn't engage with the pressure and went straight to your own records instead.
e-safe-hangup.lesson: A refund never requires remote access to your computer or a code read aloud. Verify any charge in your own account, not with the caller.

e-safe-verify.title: You refused remote access and verified independently
e-safe-verify.explanation: You stopped at the exact point the scam needs you to comply, and moved to a channel you trust.
e-safe-verify.lesson: Hang up and call the number printed on your card or statement. Never install software or read codes because a 'billing agent' asked, even on a call you placed.

e-compromised-install.title: You installed their remote tool
e-compromised-install.explanation: With remote access they can drain accounts, steal files, and lock you out while you watch the screen.
e-compromised-install.lesson: No legitimate refund or support call needs to remote-control your computer. That request is the whole scam.

e-compromised-code.title: You read out the one-time code
e-compromised-code.explanation: That code let them log in as you or authorise a payment. Codes are for you to type, never to say.
e-compromised-code.lesson: A one-time code read aloud is a handover of your account. Legitimate staff never ask you to speak it.

e-decline.title: You chose not to call back
e-decline.explanation: An unsolicited 'you'll be charged, call this number' message is classic callback phishing (TOAD). Not calling is a valid, safe choice.
e-decline.lesson: Don't call numbers from unexpected billing scares. Look up the company yourself, or check your real account.

red_flags.title: Unsolicited payment scare
red_flags.explanation: A surprise 'you'll be charged $499' with a number to call is designed to make you phone back in a panic. This is callback phishing, also called TOAD.

red_flags.title: Remote-access request
red_flags.explanation: Being told to install a 'support tool' so they can connect to your computer is a hallmark of refund and tech-support scams.

red_flags.title: One-time code request
red_flags.explanation: Any request to read a code aloud is an attempt to take over your account or approve a payment.

what_to_do: Don't call back numbers from unexpected billing or renewal warnings. Find the company yourself and check your real account.
Never install remote-access software or read a one-time code because a caller asked, even if you placed the call.
If money may be involved, hang up and call your bank on the number printed on your card.
lesson: Callback phishing flips the script: you dial them, so it feels safe. The defence is the same, verify independently and never grant remote access or share a code.

intro: Your phone rings. The screen shows "IT Service Desk".

n1.speaker: caller
lines: Hi, this is Marcus from the IT Service Desk. We've detected a sign-in to your account from another country and we're locking it down right now.
To confirm it's really you and stop the attacker, I need the six-digit code we just sent to your phone. Can you read it to me?

choices.label: Read the code so they can secure my account
Why would IT need my code? That's not normal
I'll hang up and call the service desk on our internal number

n2.speaker: caller
lines: I understand your caution, but the attacker is active in your account right now. If you don't confirm in the next minute you'll be locked out of everything.
Just read me the code, or approve the prompt I'm sending to your phone now.

choices.label: Approve the prompt to make it stop
No. I'm hanging up and contacting IT myself

e-code.title: You read the code to the caller
e-code.explanation: They used it to log in as you. 'IT Service Desk' on your screen is trivially spoofed and proves nothing.
e-code.lesson: Real IT never needs a code you received. Hang up and reach the service desk through a channel you already trust.

e-approve.title: You approved the login prompt
e-approve.explanation: Approving a prompt you didn't start let the attacker straight in. The 'emergency' was manufactured to rush you.
e-approve.lesson: Only approve prompts you started yourself. An unexpected prompt means your password is already known, so deny it and report.

e-callback.title: You hung up and verified through IT
e-callback.explanation: You refused to act on the caller's urgency and used a trusted channel to check instead.
e-callback.lesson: Caller ID is easy to fake. Hang up and call back on a number you already have before doing anything a caller asks.

e-decline.title: You let it go and checked with IT yourself
e-decline.explanation: Declining an unexpected 'urgent IT' call and verifying independently is exactly right.
e-decline.lesson: If it is genuinely urgent, IT can be reached on your known internal number. Spoofed caller ID can't survive a callback.

red_flags.title: Spoofed caller ID
red_flags.explanation: The name and number on screen are not proof of identity; attackers fake 'IT Service Desk' easily.

red_flags.title: Request for your code or approval
red_flags.explanation: Asking you to read a code or approve a prompt is an attempt to complete the attacker's own login as you.

red_flags.title: Manufactured emergency
red_flags.explanation: 'An attacker is active right now, act immediately' is pressure to stop you thinking and verifying.

what_to_do: Hang up on unexpected 'urgent IT or security' calls and call the service desk back on your known internal number.
Never read out a one-time code or approve a login prompt you didn't start.
Report the call so IT can warn others and check your account.
lesson: A caller claiming to be IT, a code request, and a ticking clock is vishing. Hang up and call a number you already trust.
